item.content:encoded:
I never said the jokes were not there, I just had absolutely no idea what they were supposed to do. I suppose I'm a bit at fault for phrasing it poorly — I essentially said "Where are the jokes in this article?", when what I meant was "What is supposed to make this article funny?". Having the list of jokes laid out for me is nice, but a collection of jokes all put on one page in one format does not an SCP-J make.

The problem here is that the main idea of the article is too obtuse to be funny. The recovery log, upon review, has potential. If the point here is to mock your 2000 contest entry, it's too narrow to work as a joke entry for me. If you want to effectively poke fun at conventions of the format as the whole, you can't devote the containment procedures to Star Wars jokes and play the description straight and expect people to immediately view it as a cohesive piece and understand what you're getting at.

This is the seed of a clever idea, but it just dicks around for too long without actually touching upon it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-joke
http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SelfReferentialHumor
http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DeconstructedTrope
http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreakingTheFourthWall

TL;DR: It turns out that in the years since Vaudeville, humans have invented other forms of humor than just Shaggy Dog Stories. I'm not sure how you've managed to be on the internet for this long without ever encountering any of them, but they're out there, they're funny, and they inform many of the -Js where people ask what the joke is.

I humbly encourage you to do your own research and expose yourself to as many different forms of humor as you can, so that you can form your own opinion prior to considering mine:

Things what I thought was teh funny.
But they say any joke you have to explain...


Before we even get to the article, you really have to give at least some credit to the gif. I pasted this thing into chat in Site-19 when people were generally posting links to pictures, and this got an instant reaction. It's pretty obvious why. The dog looks ridiculous. Look at those clown shoes. And it doesn't even realize there's anything odd about its appearance at all, it just wants that food. I call it cute in the article, but if I'm honest there's a pinch of Uncanny Valley in there. More than anything though, the dog just looks derpy and awkward.

Special Containment Procedures are pretty dry, as they usually are. The first joke I can spot is referential. The AT-AT class vehicle the dog is dressed as only appeared once in the Star Wars movies, when the Empire was attacking a Rebel outpost on a frozen planet called Hoth. The expectation is that the audience has seen Star Wars and at least vaguely remembers that iconic scene with the giant metal camels stomping towards the camera. I did not think this expectation was too far outside of the mainstream. Assuming the Hoth scene is in your mind, you should have an idea where this is going the instant you read the word "snow." Audience anticipation of the skip running amok with lasers is the punchline.

The next joke doesn't occur until the third paragraph. Again, it relies on the movie that informs it for context. In the movie, outgunned and outmatched Rebel pilots managed to take down one of the mechs by entangling their legs in a tow cable. If you don't remember this scene, I suspect you haven't either seen or else don't remember the original Star Wars Trilogy. (The first three movies in chronological order of release, not "Episode 1, Episode 2, and Episode 3.) If that's the case, I dunno but maybe consider watching them. They're pretty much broadly considered a touchstone of western civilization at this point.

Kissing noises and holding treats to attract dogs. Man, you ever own a dog? That trick NEVER works, unless the dog was done exploring and ready to come home anyway. But everybody tries it. It's just instinctive. Human nature. It's a bad plan that we all come up with, and to people who already know it doesn't work, it just looks ridiculous whenever somebody tries it. Now picture a bunch of PHDs in lab coats out in a field doing it at the same time. You know how when somebody really intelligent or dignified does something stupid like slip on a banana peel, it's a million times funnier than when a regular person does it? That principle is at work here. It's bad advice, that the audience knows is bad advice, but the preparer of the document doesn't. If you didn't get this joke, you're either not a dog owner, or else you've been a dog owner for so long you don't remember a time when you weren't good with dogs yet and you made a rookie mistake and the dog got out. Or, hell, I don't know, maybe you just let your dogs run loose and don't even bother with leash laws. I sure hope not. That's a good way to lose your dog.

Dogs are cute. Humans are irrational around cute dogs. That could be mistaken as a memetic effect. We've checked. It isn't. Which is a good thing, because dude preparing the report sounds like he's infected. Maybe it wouldn't hurt to put a little note here about what to do if you *suspect* you're infected. The author of the report's internal conflict exposes the humor of the situation, which is rooted in human nature (dogs look cute to us) at odds with the mission of the Foundation (The Foundation is Cold.) Yes, toher animal skips have done this before. No, I don't think it's possible to do a "pet" skip without at least giving it a nod. It is not the focus of this piece. It is, however, a neccessary component, and I feel I gave it a justifiably novel treatment this time.

Contingency plan for if the skip gets into the snow. This one isn't funny so much, except inasmuch as it averts expectations. The dog doesn't just run around hog wild shooting lasers everywhere, it just does what the AT-ATs do in the movie. It walks in a straight line laying down covering fire. This makes containing such an ostensibly dangerous skip almost laughably easy.

The Description is played Straight, except for the last line. Heh heh. Farts.

And of course, this brings us to the Recovery Log. We break the fourth wall entirely and just berate the audience for wanting to read a depressing story where "There Are No Happy Endings." I deliberately write the most overwrought, depressing, innocence-defiling ending I can possibly think of, which in my mind counts as… is it parody or satire? I'm making fun of the conventions of a fictional work, so I guess it's Parody.

Sorry I had to spend this much text defending what was essentially a throwaway IRC gag, but every time I or somebody else posts a new -J, it seems like there's always one person going "Where's the Joke?" So, here. HERE are the jokes. But don't take my word for it. Look above you. Jyggalag and Randomini get it. They got it way back in the IRC channel when I first pasted the picture. Like it or not, these jokes exist. You can argue that you don't find them funny, or that they're not your style, or that they depend too heavily on prior awareness of Star Wars to connect with general audiences, but you can't just pretend they're not there.
